chapters: What holds up, and what doesn't

units.t: Attachment Styles in Adult Life.
Part one. From orphanages to the lab.
If you've spent any time on social media lately, you've probably seen someone described as anxiously attached, or a partner dismissed as avoidant.
Attachment styles have become one of the most popular ideas in modern psychology.
Some of it is solid science.
Some of it has drifted a long way from the research.
Let's walk through where the idea came from, what actually holds up, and what's closer to a horoscope.
The story begins with a British psychiatrist called John Bowlby.
In the years after the Second World War, Bowlby studied children who had been separated from their parents, some in hospitals, some in orphanages, some evacuated from cities during the bombing.
In 1951 he wrote a report for the World Health Organization on children who had lost their families.
His conclusion was that a warm, continuous relationship with a caregiver wasn't a luxury.
It was as important to a young child's development as food.
That sounds obvious now.
At the time it wasn't.
Many experts believed babies loved their mothers mainly because mothers fed them.
Affection was treated as a side effect of being fed.
Hospital visiting hours for parents of sick children were often strictly limited, partly on the theory that visits upset the children.
Evidence against the feeding theory came from an American psychologist, Harry Harlow, in a set of experiments that are hard to hear about today.
Harlow raised baby rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers.
One was made of bare wire and held a bottle of milk.
The other was covered in soft cloth but gave no food.
The babies went to the wire mother to feed, then spent most of their time clinging to the cloth one.
When something frightened them, they ran to the cloth mother, not the one with the milk.
Harlow published his findings in 1958 under the title The Nature of Love.
Comfort, it turned out, was a need in its own right.
Bowlby pulled these threads together into what became attachment theory.
His central idea was that children are born with a drive to stay close to a trusted person, especially when they're scared, tired or unwell.
That person acts as a safe haven to return to when things go wrong, and a secure base to explore the world from when things are fine.
Bowlby didn't think this faded in childhood.
He wrote that attachment is part of human life from the cradle to the grave.
The person who turned this theory into something you could measure was Mary Ainsworth, an American-Canadian psychologist who had worked with Bowlby in London.
After watching mothers and babies in Uganda and later in Baltimore, she designed a short laboratory procedure known as the Strange Situation.
A baby of around one year old plays in an unfamiliar room with their mother.
A stranger comes in.
The mother slips out for a few minutes, then returns.
Later the baby is left completely alone for a short time, and then the mother comes back again.
What Ainsworth watched most closely wasn't the crying when the mother left.
It was the reunion.
Most babies in her studies were upset by the separation, went straight to their mother when she returned, were comforted quickly, and then went back to playing.
She called them secure.
Some babies barely seemed to react to the separation, and tended to ignore their mother or turn away when she came back.
Yet later research found that babies like these often had raised heart rates during separations.
They were stressed.
They just weren't showing it.
She called them avoidant.
A smaller group were very distressed and hard to settle, seeking comfort while also pushing it away.
She called them resistant, or ambivalent.
Later, the researchers Mary Main and Judith Solomon described a fourth pattern, called disorganised, in which babies seemed to have no consistent way of coping at all.
So those are the roots.
Secure, avoidant and anxious started as descriptions of one-year-olds in a playroom.
In the next part, we'll see how they jumped from babies to grown-up romance, and what happened to them along the way.
Part two. The leap to adult love.
In 1987, two researchers at the University of Denver, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver, had a bold idea.
What if romantic love was the adult version of the bond Bowlby and Ainsworth had studied in babies?
A partner, after all, is often the person we turn to when we're frightened or hurting, and the base we venture out from.
To test it, they ran what they called a love quiz in a local newspaper.
Readers were asked to pick which of three short paragraphs best described their feelings in close relationships.
One described finding it fairly easy to get close to others and not worrying much about being abandoned.
One described feeling uncomfortable being close and finding it hard to trust.
The third described wanting to get closer than partners seemed to want, and worrying that a partner didn't really love them.
The results lined up remarkably well with the proportions in Ainsworth's baby studies.
A little over half of the readers chose the secure description.
About a quarter chose the avoidant one.
And about a fifth chose the anxious one.
The secure group also described their most important love relationships as happier, more trusting and longer lasting.
The paper sparked a whole new field of research.
Since then, the ideas have been refined in two important ways.
The first came in 1991, when Kim Bartholomew, working with Leonard Horowitz, pointed out that there seemed to be two different kinds of avoidance.
Some avoidant people seemed genuinely content to be self-reliant.
She called that dismissing.
Others seemed to want closeness but feared it, keeping people at a distance to avoid being hurt.
She called that fearful.
That's where the four adult styles you often hear about come from.
The second refinement matters even more, and it's the part pop psychology usually leaves out.
When researchers measured attachment with long questionnaires rather than a single choice, the results didn't fall into neat boxes.
Instead, they spread out along two separate sliding scales.
One scale is attachment anxiety, which is how much you worry about rejection and whether people will be there for you.
The other is attachment avoidance, which is how uncomfortable you are with closeness and depending on others.
Everyone sits somewhere on both scales.
Someone low on both would be described as secure.
Someone high on anxiety but low on avoidance fits the old anxious label.
The psychologist Chris Fraley and his colleagues have tested this with statistical methods designed to tell true categories from smooth scales.
Their work suggests attachment works more like height than like blood type.
There's no line where you stop being secure and become anxious.
There's just more or less of each tendency.
Researchers also distinguish two quite different ways of measuring adult attachment.
Social psychologists mostly use questionnaires about romantic relationships.
Developmental psychologists often use a long interview, called the Adult Attachment Interview, about how a person talks about their own childhood.
These two methods overlap far less than you might expect, which is a good reminder that attachment in adults isn't one simple thing sitting inside us.
If you'd like to try the idea on yourself, you can do it purely by ear.
If you're driving, keep your eyes on the road and just let these sit in the back of your mind.
When someone you love doesn't reply for hours, how much does it bother you?
That's a rough sense of the anxiety scale.
And when a partner or close friend wants to talk about feelings, or needs to lean on you, how comfortable is that?
That's a rough sense of the avoidance scale.
Most people land somewhere in the middle on both, and that's perfectly normal.
So the science is richer and less boxy than the labels.
In the final part, we'll sort what holds up from what's been oversold.
Part three. What holds up, and what doesn't.
Let's start with what the research genuinely supports.
People differ in how anxious and how avoidant they tend to be in close relationships, and those differences are measurable.
They're linked, on average, with real outcomes.
People lower on both scales tend to report more satisfying relationships, handle conflict more constructively, and seek and give support more easily.
Those links show up across many studies and many countries.
There's also good evidence that these tendencies come alive under stress.
When people feel threatened, the attachment system switches on.
Someone high in anxiety tends to reach out more and seek reassurance.
Someone high in avoidance tends to pull back and handle things alone.
When life is calm, these differences are much less noticeable.
Now for the more doubtful claims.
The first is that your attachment style is set in early childhood and stays with you for life.
The evidence here is mixed.
Some long-term studies that followed babies into adulthood found a fair amount of continuity.
Others found almost none.
When Chris Fraley combined the results in 2002, he found a real but modest link between attachment in infancy and later in life.
In plain terms, your early years matter, but they are not a sentence.
Adult attachment also shifts with experience.
A long, steady relationship with a dependable partner tends to nudge people towards security over time.
A painful betrayal or divorce can push the other way.
Researchers use the lovely term earned security for people who describe a difficult childhood but have become secure as adults, often through good relationships or good therapy.
The second doubtful claim is that attachment explains everything about a relationship.
It doesn't.
It's one influence among many, alongside personality, stress, money, health, communication skills and plain compatibility.
A relationship that isn't working isn't necessarily an attachment problem, and a secure person can still pick a poor match.
Even the strongest links in this research are averages across large groups.
They can't tell you how any one couple will fare.
The third is the habit of diagnosing other people.
Popular books, the best known being Attached by Amir Levine and Rachel Heller, published in 2010, have helped many readers put words to patterns in their relationships.
But online, the language often turns into a way of labelling a partner after an argument.
Calling someone avoidant because they wanted a quiet night in isn't science.
It's a judgement wearing a lab coat.
The research measures tendencies across lots of situations, not single moments, and it certainly doesn't sort people into good and bad partners.
The fourth is a simple mix-up of names.
Attachment parenting, the approach linked with things like baby-wearing and co-sleeping, is a separate parenting philosophy.
It borrows the word, but it isn't what Bowlby and Ainsworth studied, and the research doesn't show that you need those particular practices to raise a securely attached child.
What mattered in Ainsworth's work was responsiveness.
Noticing what a child needs, and reliably responding, most of the time.
Not perfectly.
Most of the time.
So what can you do with all this?
If you recognise yourself as higher on anxiety, it can help to notice the moment the alarm goes off, like an unanswered message.
Then remind yourself that silence usually means busy, not leaving.
If you lean towards avoidance, it can help to notice the urge to withdraw when someone needs you, and to stay present a little longer than feels natural.
And in any relationship, the thing that builds security is the same thing Ainsworth saw in those playrooms.
Being there, reliably, when it counts.
If patterns like these are causing real distress, talking with a counsellor can help, and Relationships Australia is one well-known place to start.
To sum up, attachment theory grew from serious research on children and was extended to adult love in 1987.
The best evidence treats it as two sliding scales, anxiety and avoidance, rather than fixed types.
And your style isn't destiny, because experiences and relationships can shift it towards security.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What was the name of Mary Ainsworth's laboratory procedure for studying babies' attachment?
Answer. The Strange Situation.
Question two. Modern research measures adult attachment on two scales. What are they?
Answer. Anxiety and avoidance.
Question three. What do researchers call it when someone with a difficult childhood becomes secure as an adult?
Answer. Earned security.
That's the end of Attachment Styles in Adult Life. Thanks for listening. Go easy on the labels.
